\begin{example} \end{example}[Euclidean metric in polar coordinates]

Source: petersen:page-0034 ↗ def:pet-ch1-coordinate-metric ↗ ex:pet-ch1-euclidean-coords

1. ch1:1.4.2On the complement of a half-line in $\mathbb {R}^2$, polar coordinates give \[ g=dr^2+r^2d\theta ^2. \] Thus $g_{rr}=1$, $g_{r\theta }=g_{\theta r}=0$, and $g_{\theta \theta }=r^2$. \end{example}
Proof

↗ ex:pet-ch1-polar-coords

\sketch From $x=r\cos \theta $ and $y=r\sin \theta $,

\[ dx=\cos \theta \, dr-r\sin \theta \, d\theta , \qquad dy=\sin \theta \, dr+r\cos \theta \, d\theta . \]

Expanding $dx^2+dy^2$ cancels the mixed terms and yields $dr^2+r^2d\theta ^2$.
